title: Christological nature and the incarnation
english: The Spirit worked again, and it did so in a divinely fitting manner, giving itself to those who believe in Him.
In this, God and man were the same person, and the one who acknowledges the sandal is not worthy to untie it, let alone be compared to the divine essence.
As it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son; I have today begotten you' (Psalm 2:7).

Cyril explains that the Son, who alone knows the Father and is known by the Father alone, is the Wisdom and the Word of God, and the Angel of the great counsel, and that He clearly explains to us the mystery of the economy with flesh through the voice of the prophet.

The Son, being by nature and truly the Son of God, and having taken on the essence of God and the Father, became flesh, that is, man, according to the voice of John, and He has become a brother to those on earth, having undergone birth according to the flesh with us.
Although He is eternal and has always co-existed with the Father, He became flesh, and as the unique Son, He is seen by the Father, who says, 'You are my Son; I have today begotten you.'

This statement shows the manifest confession, namely the exaltation, and the phrase 'You are my Son' establishes His eternal nature, while the phrase 'I have today begotten you' reveals His birth according to the flesh, which He willingly underwent through the Holy Virgin; and for this reason she is named Theotokos.
We must beware, lest what is said in the prophets comes upon us: 'Behold, the scorners, and marvel, and be vanished…'
Cyril says, 'Behold, the scorners, and look upon; and how the rough thing is cut off.'
The Lord warns us that what was said to others should not come upon us.
For the Lord has commanded us, 'I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you might be for salvation unto the ends of the earth' (Acts 13:47).

Christ shone upon the Gentiles, leaving under the heavens a light infused with divinity, so that the divine nature and the higher realms might be beheld by eyes of pure intellect, and the ways of spiritual worship might be established.
When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their garments and leaped into the crowd, shouting and crying out.
It is the custom of the Jews to tear their garments at blasphemies against God, as Caiaphas did when Christ called Himself the Son of God, shouting aloud and saying, 'He has blasphemed!'!

The godly disciples Paul and Barnabas also did this in Lycaonia, where they became known; for some had wandered from the passion, and the matter was paradoxical to those watching, and the observers desired to offer sacrifices to them as signs of divinity, saying, 'The gods, having been made like unto men, have come to us.'
They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he was, as they said, the leader of the word.
translator_notes: The text contains several repetitions of the Psalm quote and the name Cyril, likely due to the nature of the source manuscript or compilation.
p12 'Γεγόνασι μὲν ἐν Λυκαονίᾳ' is a fragment; it likely means 'They became [known/famous] in Lycaonia'.

title: Critique of Legalistic Burden and Call to Inner Repentance
english: Since the action undertaken was regarded as a kind of disgrace, they tore their garments, following Jewish traditions and written customs. Moreover, the custom itself is slandered as not deriving from the law and being altogether lawless. Indeed, the God of all things spoke to those who were shaping such practices and turning far from true piety, saying to the Jews: 'Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and lamentation; tear your hearts, and not your garments.'

Now then, what are you trying to do, placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples? . . . Cyril. Furthermore, since the law is burdensome and hard to bear, the godly disciples have truly confessed this, reproaching certain forms of ignorance. For they said: 'Now then, what are you trying? And the following things.' This is the same point: the law is admittedly burdensome to those of Israel, and the godly disciples agreed to this as well. The Savior himself taught us this, saying: 'Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.' Yet he describes those who labor and are burdened under the law as such, while he himself calls himself gentle, not claiming this quality comes from the law. As it is written, after these things I will return and rebuild the tent of David that has fallen. . . . Cyril. The tent of David signifies the race of the Jews.
translator_notes: Fragments at [p6]-[p9] and [p22]-[p25] contain only letters with no clear words (τ., λ., Κυρίλλου); these are treated as edge cuts and not translated. The numeral '74.772' at [p6] appears to be a folio or section marker and is omitted as non-content. Stray digits and edition headers (like ΤΟΜΟΣ Β΄) were not present in the locked Greek, so none were skipped. The Greek is complete within the given clauses; no mid-word cuts occurred in translatable text.

The phrase 'πραΰς' in [p19] uses a variant spelling with iota subscript; the lemma is standardized to πραΰς for glossing. The perfect passive διαβεβλήται in [p2] is rendered as 'is slandered' to reflect the ongoing state of accusation. The repetition of 'Νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε;' in [p6] and [p12] is treated as a refrain and translated consistently in both instances.

All supplied clauses have been translated; no summaries or omissions were made. The english paragraphs follow the author's voice and claims, rephrasing the source word order into natural literary prose while preserving every idea from the pass_a_gloss.

title: Faith and Works
english: The Lord called them fools, saying that those who claim to be wise have become foolish. He knew that after his departure, false teachers would arise, and so the Holy Spirit, keeping us safe, warns us against the ravings of heretics. In the early days, it was customary for ships to have symbols of the Dioscuri, which were considered foreign and possibly idolatrous, as Isaiah says, they will sail in foreign ships, navigating the sea (Isaiah 60:9). 'Let him ask in faith, with no doubting' (James 1:6). Cyril: The one who doubts is plainly insolent. For if you did not believe that he will fulfill your request, you should not have come at all, so as not to be found accusing the Almighty by being double-minded against your will. So we must refuse so shameful a sickness. 'Do you want to know, you empty man, that faith without works is dead? Abraham our father...' (James 2:20–21). Cyril, from the Letter to the Romans: Since the blessed James says that Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac his son on the altar, while Paul says that he was justified by faith, the apparent contradiction is to be understood this way: before he had Isaac he believed, and he received Isaac as the reward of his faith; yet when he offered Isaac on the altar, he not only did the work he was commanded but also did not let go of his faith, reckoning that in Isaac his seed would multiply like the stars, and that God is able even to raise from the dead. Yet Paul makes the blessed David, a man famous for piety, a witness and helper of his own words, and wisely sets forth, as in the Spirit, the forgiveness that comes through faith and announces it to all people; for he knew that it would be present in Christ in due time. 'You see that faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made complete' (James 2:22). Cyril: He was bringing the rational sacrifice, bidding the laws of nature farewell, trampling the goad of a father's unyielding love, and setting nothing earthly against his love for God. 'And Abraham believed God' (James 2:23). Cyril: So the one who honors the God and Master of all with faith has righteousness as his prize. 'If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well' (James 3:2).
